state.misconception_label: Assumes that an arrow on a number line starts at zero

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: ![Number line with -12 and -7 marked. Starting at -12, follow an arrow pointing to the right labelled +10. Then there is an arrow labelled b pointing to the left, which ends at -7 on the number line.]() What is the value of \( b \) ? I got \( -7 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of the number line as a journey. Starting at -12, you move 10 steps to the right. Then you need to move back in the opposite direction to reach -7. What number do you land on if you take those steps?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, so if I start at -12 and move 10 steps to the right, I think I land on -2. But then if I have to go back to -7, I’m not sure how to figure out what \( b \) is. Do I just count how many steps I need to go back from -2 to -7?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of the number line like a road trip. You started at -12 and drove 10 miles to the right, landing at -2. Now, when you drive back to -7, you need to think about the total distance you traveled, not just the last segment. What would be the total number of miles you drove from -12 to -7?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, so I think I get it a bit better now. If I start at -12 and go to -2, that’s 10 steps to the right. Then from -2 to -7, I have to go back 5 steps. So, does that mean \( b \) is -5? But I’m still confused about how to figure out the value of \( b \) from that. Can you help me with that?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses journey metaphors but never directly addresses the student's misconception about arrows starting at zero, and introduces confusing language about 'total distance' that conflates the problem; the student does improve from -7 to -5 but remains confused about what b represents.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete real-world analogies (journey, road trip with miles driven) to ground the abstract number line problem in everyday experiences, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
